title: Chapter XXVII
focus: a journey and a mercenary suitor

teacherSummary.text: Elizabeth sets out for Hunsford with Sir William and Maria Lucas, stopping in London with the Gardiners. Discussing Wickham's pursuit of Miss King, Elizabeth and Mrs. Gardiner debate the line between prudence and greed. The Gardiners invite Elizabeth on a summer tour.

vocabulary.definition: To mix in a confused mass
vocabulary.context: Lakes, mountains, and rivers, shall not be jumbled together in our imaginations; nor, when we attempt to describe any particular scene, will we begin quarrelling about its relative situation.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “jumble”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: “Her not objecting, does not justify him.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “object”: ob- (Latin ob, "against, toward") + ject (Latin iacere, "to throw"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: Distinguished by various forms, or by a variety of aspects or objects
vocabulary.context: With no greater events than these in the Longbourn family, and otherwise diversified by little beyond the walks to Meryton, sometimes dirty and sometimes cold, did January and February pass away.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “diversified”: vers (Latin vertere, "to turn") + -ed (Old English -ed, past or "having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To collect, and reduce to order, as troops dispersed or thrown into confusion
vocabulary.context: Gardiner then rallied her niece on Wickham’s desertion, and complimented her on bearing it so well.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “rally”: -ly (Old English -lice, "in the manner of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I should be sorry to think our friend mercenary.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “mercenary”: -ary (Latin -arius, "connected with"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being shy
vocabulary.context: On the stairs were a troop of little boys and girls, whose eagerness for their cousin’s appearance would not allow them to wait in the drawing-room, and whose shyness, as they had not seen her for a twelvemonth, prevented their coming lower.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “shyness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: An edifice in which dramatic performances or spectacles are exhibited for the amusement of spectators
vocabulary.context: The day passed most pleasantly away; the morning in bustle and shopping, and the evening at one of the theatres.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “theatre”: the (Greek theos, "god"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Absence had increased her desire of seeing Charlotte again, and weakened her disgust of Mr.

vocabulary.definition: To carry or bear from one place to another
vocabulary.context: Oh! what hours of transport we shall spend!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “transport”: trans- (Latin trans, "across") + port (Latin portare, "to carry"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: In exact or careful conformity to truth, or to some standard of requirement, the result of care or pains
vocabulary.context: And when we do return, it shall not be like other travellers, without being able to give one accurate idea of anything.

vocabulary.etymology: “accurate”: ac- (Latin ad, "to") + cur (Latin cura, "care") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXVII,” how does Austen show a journey and a mercenary suitor? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXVII develops the idea of a journey and a mercenary suitor. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XXVII to complicate the reader's understanding of a journey and a mercenary suitor. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXVII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of a journey and a mercenary suitor responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXVII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of a journey and a mercenary suitor. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: It was a journey of only twenty-four miles, and they began it so early as to be in Gracechurch-street by noon. As they drove to Mr. Gardiner’s door, Jane was at a drawing-room window watching their arrival; when they entered the passage she was there to welcome them, and Elizabeth, looking earnestly in her face, was pleased to see it healthful and lovely as ever. On the stairs were a troop of little boys and girls, whose eagerness for their cousin’s appearance would not allow them to wait in the drawing-room, and whose shyness, as they had not seen her for a twelvemonth, prevented their coming lower. All was joy and kindness. The day passed most pleasantly away; the morning in bustle and shopping, and the evening at one of the theatres.

options: A journey and a mercenary suitor

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Where is the line between a prudent marriage and a mercenary one? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are jumbled, objecting, diversified, rallied, mercenary. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Lakes, mountains, and rivers, shall not be jumbled together in our imaginations; nor, when we attempt to describe any particular scene, will we begin quarrelling about its relative situation.” Webster's says: To mix in a confused mass. Now the word history: “jumble”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “object”: ob- (Latin ob, "against, toward") + ject (Latin iacere, "to throw"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “diversified”: vers (Latin vertere, "to turn") + -ed (Old English -ed, past or "having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Travel by post-chaise required overnight stops; families relied on relatives in town. Why does this chapter matter? The debate about 'mercenary' versus 'prudent' motives sharpens the theme of marriage and money. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to a journey and a mercenary suitor.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
